deep.reconstruction:
PART 1. General partial-fraction integral.

Gauss heads the page with ∫ x^{m-1} dx/(1+x^k) (the image shows a stray/ambiguous exponent n; the right-hand side is independent of n, so effectively n=1). He writes it as a sum over the odd multiples θ_j=(2j+1)π/k:

∫ x^{m-1}/(1+x^k) dx = -(2/k) Σ_j cos(mθ_j) · log √(1-2x cosθ_j + x²) + (2/k) Σ_j sin(mθ_j) · arctan( x sinθ_j / (1 - x cosθ_j) ).

The sum runs over θ = π/k, 3π/k, …, iπ/k, with i the last odd number.

Implicit basis (mine): 1+x^k = ∏_j (x² - 2x cosθ_j + 1) for k even. Decomposing into partial fractions and integrating each quadratic factor gives one log term and one arctan term. The arctan is written in the form arctan(x sinθ/(1-x cosθ)), which equals arg(1 - x e^{-iθ}) and vanishes at x=0, so the whole expression is the integral from 0 to x.

PART 2. Application to ∫ dp/(1-p⁴)^{1/4}.

Substitution ("posito"): 1-p⁴ = p⁴x⁴, i.e. x = ((1-p⁴)/p⁴)^{1/4}, equivalently p = (1+x⁴)^{-1/4}. The following steps are mine:
- dp = -x³(1+x⁴)^{-5/4} dx.
- (1-p⁴)^{1/4} = px = x(1+x⁴)^{-1/4}.
- Hence dp/(1-p⁴)^{1/4} = -x² dx/(1+x⁴).

So the integral is reduced to the case k=4, m=3 of Part 1. With θ=π/4 and 3π/4 this gives

F(x) := ∫_0^x x²dx/(1+x⁴) = (1/4)√(1/2) · log[(1-x√2+x²)/(1+x√2+x²)] + (1/2)√(1/2) · arctan[x√2/(1-x²)].

This is exactly what Gauss writes. The two arctan terms of the general formula combine by the tangent addition theorem: arctan(x/(√2-x)) + arctan(x/(√2+x)) = arctan(√2x/(1-x²)).

He then rewrites the arctan as an arccos. Since cos²φ = (1-x²)²/(1+x⁴) for φ = arctan(√2x/(1-x²)), the arctan equals arccos[(1-x²)/√(1+x⁴)]. This form gives the continuous branch 0≤φ≤π for all x≥0, which is the point of the rewriting, since the arctan form jumps at x=1.

"Also x=0 | 0, x=∞ | [struck]" tabulates the end values:
- F(0) = 0.
- F(∞) = π/(2√2) ≈ 1.11072, using the arccos branch.
- Since p runs 0→1 as x runs ∞→0, ∫_0^p dp/(1-p⁴)^{1/4} = F(∞) - F(x(p)) (my completion).

"Also für p=0,8": p⁴ = 0.4096, so x⁴ = 0.5904/0.4096 = 5904/4096 and x ≈ 1.09571. The page stops here. Completing it (mine): F(x) ≈ -0.30954 + 0.60087 = 0.29133, so ∫_0^{0.8} dp/(1-p⁴)^{1/4} ≈ 1.11072 - 0.29133 = 0.81939. This agrees with the binomial series 0.8 + 0.8⁵/20 + 5·0.8⁹/288 + … ≈ 0.81938.

This is a numerical exercise in evaluating a pseudo-elliptic (elementary) quarter-power integral. It sits next to the lemniscatic and elliptic material on the neighbouring page.
errors: The exponent 'n' in the heading ∫ x^{m-1}dx/((1+x^k))^n is inconsistent with the right-hand side, which is valid only for n=1. It is probably a stray mark or slip.

The general formula as written (log and arctan terms over odd multiples iπ/k) is complete only for k even. For k odd the last factor is (1+x), and its term should be (1/k)(-1)^{m-1} log(1+x). Applying the same pattern with i=k would give twice this. Gauss's '&c' leaves this implicit.
The formula holds for 0 < m < k, with the integral taken from 0. This is unstated.
Sign/limits: ∫ dp/(1-p⁴)^{1/4} = -∫ x²dx/(1+x⁴). Gauss writes +F(x) without the minus sign or the constant F(∞). His subsequent endpoint table (x=0, x=∞) suggests he intended ∫_0^p = F(∞) - F(x).

The arccos form as written, (1/2)√(1/2) arccos[(1-xx)²/(1+x⁴)], is incorrect literally. The correct form is arccos[(1-x²)/√(1+x⁴)], i.e. the square root of what is written, since (1-x²)²/(1+x⁴) = cos²φ. It is probably a missing radical or shorthand. An alternative correct form is (1/4)√(1/2) arccos[(1-4x²+x⁴)/(1+x⁴)].

results.what: Closed form of ∫ x^{m-1}dx/(1+x^k) as a sum of log and arctan terms over the angles (2j+1)π/k
results.modern_name: Partial-fraction integration of x^{m-1}/(1+x^k) (Cotes factorization of 1+x^k)
results.usually_credited_to: Cotes (Harmonia mensurarum, 1722) and de Moivre; Euler (Institutiones calculi integralis, 1768)

results.what: Reduction of ∫ dp/(1-p⁴)^{1/4} to ∫ x²dx/(1+x⁴) via 1-p⁴ = p⁴x⁴, giving an elementary log + arctan closed form
results.modern_name: Rationalizing substitution for a binomial (Chebyshev-integrable) differential / pseudo-elliptic integral
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (binomial integrals); Chebyshev 1853 for the general integrability criterion

results.what: Endpoint value F(∞) = ∫_0^∞ x²/(1+x⁴) dx = π/(2√2) and numerical evaluation at p=0.8 (x⁴ = 5904/4096)
results.modern_name: Beta-function integral ∫_0^∞ x^{m-1}/(1+x^k) dx = π/(k sin(mπ/k))

deep.surprise_reason: Standard 18th-century integral calculus (Cotes/Euler partial fractions and a binomial-differential substitution), applied to a numerical evaluation. Its only interest is as evidence of Gauss's early computational work around quartic and lemniscatic integrals. Nothing here goes beyond Euler.
